subject: ss-gastroenterology
title: Eosinophilic, infectious and corrosive oesophageal disease

steps.tx: **Eosinophilic esophagitis** is the diagnosis when swallowing is difficult and biopsies show at least **15 eosinophils per high-power field**, once other causes of oesophageal eosinophilia are set aside. Adults usually describe dysphagia or a food bolus that sticks. Sample the distal and the mid oesophagus, because a single hot biopsy under-calls the count. A proton pump inhibitor may still be used as treatment, but a response to it no longer creates a separate disease.
steps.say: Eosinophilic esophagitis needs oesophageal symptoms plus at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field, after other causes are excluded. Take biopsies from the distal and mid oesophagus. A proton pump inhibitor can still be treatment. It no longer is a separate disease.

vis.alt: Endoscopic rings, linear furrows and whitish exudates, beside a mucosa packed with eosinophils.
vis.caption: Endoscopic and histologic pattern of eosinophilic esophagitis. StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **EREFS** score, short for the endoscopic reference score, grades activity across **5** features. **Edema** is loss of the vascular markings. Rings are fixed concentric ridges, also called **trachealization**. Exudates are white plaques. Furrows are vertical lines. Strictures narrow the lumen and explain bolus impaction. The score does not replace histology, but it tells you how severe the oesophagus looks before you dilate.
steps.say: EREFS grades five endoscopic features: edema, rings or trachealization, exudates, furrows and strictures. It is a way to describe severity. Histology still makes the diagnosis, and a stricture is the finding that explains a stuck bolus.

steps.tx: **Dupilumab** is a monoclonal antibody against the **interleukin-4 receptor alpha**. Blocking that receptor stops both interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signals, which is why one drug covers two cytokines numbered 4 and 13. It is used for eosinophilic esophagitis that has not responded to swallowed steroids or dilation. It is not the first tablet you start, and it does not replace dilation of a tight stricture.
steps.say: Dupilumab blocks the interleukin-4 receptor alpha, so both interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signals fall. It is reserved for eosinophilic esophagitis that swallowed steroids and dilation have not controlled. A fibrotic stricture still needs dilation.

left.title: Swallowed steroid first
points: Fluticasone or budesonide to the mucosa.
Candida in the oesophagus is the local cost.

right.title: Dupilumab when that fails
points: Does not open a fixed stricture by itself.

steps.tx: Swallowed topical steroids are first-line drug treatment. **Fluticasone propionate** from an inhaler is puffed and swallowed, not inhaled. **Budesonide** is mixed as a viscous suspension so it coats the oesophagus. Histologic remission is reported in over **70%** of patients who take the course properly. Oral thrush and oesophageal candida are the price. Diet removal of food triggers is the non-drug partner, not a reason to skip the steroid if the oesophagus is already strictured.
steps.say: Swallowed fluticasone propionate or budesonide suspension is first-line drug treatment. Histologic remission is reported in over 70 percent when the steroid actually coats the oesophagus. Watch for candida. Diet therapy can sit beside the steroid.

rows: Puff and swallow, do not inhale
Oesophageal candida is the adverse effect

steps.tx: **Candida esophagitis** shows diffuse white plaques stuck to friable mucosa, usually in a person on steroids, antibiotics, or with weak immunity. Odynophagia is the clue, and thrush in the mouth may be absent. Treatment is oral **fluconazole** for **14 to 21** days. A patient who cannot swallow needs intravenous therapy first. Do not call every white plaque eosinophilic exudate until you have considered candida, especially after a swallowed steroid.
steps.say: Candida esophagitis is white plaques on friable mucosa, often with odynophagia and without oral thrush. Oral fluconazole for 14 to 21 days is the usual course. An intravenous azole is needed first if the patient cannot swallow.

left.title: Candida plaques
points: Diffuse white plaques, brush off with bleeding.
Host is immunosuppressed or on antibiotics.

right.title: Eosinophilic exudates
points: White specks with rings and furrows.

steps.tx: The picture shows the oesophagus lined with raised white **Candida plaques** sitting on red and **friable mucosa**. The plaques look stuck on rather than part of the wall, and the nearby lining bleeds easily. This pattern points to **Candida esophagitis**, which often follows swallowed steroids, antibiotics or weak immunity. Pain on swallowing is the usual clue. Do not mistake these plaques for the pale exudates seen with eosinophilic inflammation.
steps.say: Look at the white raised plaques coating the red oesophagus. They sit on the surface of raw friable lining that bleeds easily. This is the classic look of Candida esophagitis. It often appears after swallowed steroids or antibiotics, or when immunity is weak. Pain when swallowing is the clue, even when the mouth looks clear. Keep this apart from the pale exudates of eosinophilic disease.

vis.alt: Endoscopy of the oesophagus showing raised white Candida plaques scattered over reddened friable mucosa.
vis.caption: White Candida plaques on raw friable oesophageal lining. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Cytomegalovirus esophagitis** makes large, shallow, linear ulcers in the mid and distal oesophagus. The virus sits in endothelial and stromal cells, so the biopsy must come from the ulcer base, not the squamous edge. Nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions give the owl-eye look. Treatment is intravenous **ganciclovir**. This is a disease of transplant and advanced HIV, not of an otherwise well adult with a single Schatzki ring.
steps.say: Cytomegalovirus esophagitis causes large shallow linear ulcers. Biopsy the ulcer base, because the inclusions are in endothelial cells. Intravenous ganciclovir is the treatment in transplant recipients and in advanced HIV.

vis.alt: Enlarged cell with a dense intranuclear inclusion and a clear halo, the owl-eye pattern.
vis.caption: Owl-eye inclusion of cytomegalovirus. Public-domain micrograph, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: **Herpes simplex virus** esophagitis makes multiple small punched-out, or volcaniform, ulcers. The inclusions are in the squamous epithelium at the ulcer edge, the opposite of cytomegalovirus. Multinucleated giant cells and **Cowdry A** inclusions are the histologic names to remember. **Acyclovir** is the treatment. Severe odynophagia in a young adult can be herpes even when the immune system is intact.
steps.say: Herpes simplex virus esophagitis causes small punched-out ulcers. You should biopsy the edge for Cowdry A inclusions and multinucleated giant cells. Acyclovir is the treatment, and it can occur in a well young adult.

steps.tx: The picture shows a pale oesophagus studded with small yellow **volcaniform ulcers**, each with a **raised edge** of reddened mucosa. The ulcers sit apart from each other rather than joining into long lines. This discrete punched out pattern points to **Herpes simplex virus** infection rather than the large linear ulcers of cytomegalovirus. Sample the squamous edge for Cowdry A inclusions and multinucleated giant cells. Severe pain on swallowing in a young adult fits this picture.
steps.say: See the small scattered yellow ulcers, each with a raised red rim, on a pale oesophagus. They stay separate instead of merging into long shallow lines. That discrete volcaniform pattern favours herpes simplex virus over cytomegalovirus. Biopsy goes to the squamous edge, where Cowdry A inclusions and giant cells are found. Strong pain on swallowing in a young adult can occur even with normal immunity.

vis.alt: Endoscopy of the oesophagus showing discrete yellow volcaniform ulcers with raised red edges on pale mucosa.
vis.caption: Discrete yellow volcaniform ulcers with raised red edges. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **Zargar classification** grades acute **corrosive ingestion** injury. **Grade 0** is a normal mucosa. Grade 1 is only edema and redness. Grade 2 adds ulceration or necrosis that is not circumferential or that is circumferential but not transmural. **Grade 3**, including Grade 3b, is extensive necrosis, and Grade 3 lesions have a high stricture risk. Blind nasogastric tubes are contraindicated. Early endoscopy, done by someone who can stop, stages the injury. Do not induce vomiting.
steps.say: Zargar classification runs from Grade 0, a normal mucosa, to Grade 3b, extensive necrosis. Grade 3 lesions stricture often, and a blind nasogastric tube is contraindicated. Careful early endoscopy is how you stage the injury. Do not induce vomiting.

nodes.label: Grade 3: high stricture risk, no blind tube
